meta.description: Java Collections Framework fundamentals. Covers HashMap vs HashTable, Set vs List, and the core data structures every Java beginner must master for interviews.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and HashTable in Java?
questions.title: HashMap vs HashTable in Java
questions.direct_answer: HashMap is not synchronized (not thread-safe but faster), allows one null key and multiple null values, and is part of the Collections Framework (Java 1.2). HashTable is synchronized (thread-safe but slower), does NOT allow null keys or values, and is a legacy class (Java 1.0). In modern Java, use HashMap for single-threaded code and ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe scenarios. Nobody uses HashTable anymore.

interviewer_intent.testing: This is a classic 'do you know the Collections Framework' question. They want you to cover synchronization, null handling, and — importantly — what you'd actually use in production.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Just saying 'one is synchronized and one isn't' without mentioning ConcurrentHashMap as the modern replacement.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain WHY HashTable is obsolete — ConcurrentHashMap gives thread safety with much better performance (segment-level locking vs object-level locking). Show you know modern alternatives.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HashMap is the default choice** — not synchronized, allows one null key and multiple null values, fastest for single-threaded code
- **HashTable is legacy and dead** — synchronized on every method, no null keys/values, replaced by ConcurrentHashMap since Java 5
- **ConcurrentHashMap for thread safety** — uses bucket-level locking (Java 8+), so reads are lock-free and writes only block the affected segment
- **`Collections.synchronizedMap()` is a band-aid** — wraps any map with a full-map lock; ConcurrentHashMap is almost always a better choice
- **Initial capacity 16, load factor 0.75** — HashMap resizes when 75% full; pre-size with `new HashMap<>(expectedSize)` to avoid rehashing

This is one of the most asked Java interview questions, but the real answer goes beyond a comparison table.

**HashMap (Java 1.2 — use this):**
- Not synchronized — multiple threads can cause issues if used without external locking
- Allows ONE null key and any number of null values
- Faster because there's no synchronization overhead
- Part of the Java Collections Framework
- Iteration order is not guaranteed

**HashTable (Java 1.0 — legacy, avoid):**
- Every method is synchronized — thread-safe but painfully slow under contention
- Does NOT allow null keys or null values (throws NullPointerException)
- Legacy class that predates the Collections Framework
- Retrofitted to implement Map interface, but the design is outdated

**The real answer interviewers want to hear:** In modern Java, the choice is never between HashMap and HashTable. It's between:
- **HashMap** for single-threaded or read-mostly scenarios
- **ConcurrentHashMap** for concurrent access — it uses segment-level (or node-level in Java 8+) locking, so reads are lock-free and writes only lock the affected bucket. This is 10-100x faster than HashTable under contention.

HashTable locks the entire map for every operation. ConcurrentHashMap locks only the part being modified. That's why HashTable is effectively dead.

- HashMap: not thread-safe, allows null key/values, fast — use this by default
- HashTable: thread-safe but slow, no nulls, legacy — never use in new code
- ConcurrentHashMap: thread-safe AND fast, no nulls — use this for concurrent access
- Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) is another thread-safe option but still locks the entire map
- HashMap's initial capacity is 16 with a load factor of 0.75 — it resizes when 75% full

questions.question: When would you use a Set versus a List in Java?
questions.title: Set vs List — When to Use Which
questions.direct_answer: Use List when order matters and duplicates are allowed (e.g., a list of recent orders — same item can appear multiple times and order of purchase matters). Use Set when you need unique elements and don't care about insertion order (e.g., a set of unique user IDs who visited a page). List provides index-based access (get(5)), Set does not. Common implementations: ArrayList for List, HashSet for Set, LinkedHashSet if you need uniqueness + insertion order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can pick the right data structure based on the use case — not just define the difference.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not mentioning that Set.add() returns false if the element already exists — this is useful for deduplication logic.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Talk about a real scenario: 'I used a HashSet to track unique session IDs for analytics — O(1) contains check vs O(n) for a List'. Show you pick data structures intentionally.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **List for ordered, indexed, duplicate-allowed data** — `ArrayList` gives O(1) `get(index)` and preserves insertion order
- **Set for unique elements** — `HashSet.add()` returns `false` if the element already exists, making deduplication trivial
- **`HashSet.contains()` is O(1)** — compared to `ArrayList.contains()` at O(n), this is the key performance reason to choose Set
- **LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order** — combines uniqueness of Set with predictable iteration order
- **Custom objects need `equals()` + `hashCode()`** — Set uses both methods to determine uniqueness; missing overrides cause duplicate entries

The decision comes down to two questions: do you need duplicates, and do you need ordered access by index?

**Use a List when:**
- Duplicates are valid (`["apple", "banana", "apple"]` makes sense)
- You need to access elements by position (`list.get(3)`)
- Insertion order matters and must be preserved
- You're processing items sequentially (iterate in order)

**Use a Set when:**
- Every element must be unique (adding a duplicate is silently ignored)
- You frequently check 'does this element exist?' — `set.contains(x)` is O(1) for HashSet vs O(n) for ArrayList
- You're deduplicating data ('give me all unique countries from this list of orders')

**Choosing the implementation:**

| Need | List | Set |
|------|------|-----|
| Default choice | `ArrayList` | `HashSet` |
| Preserve insertion order | `ArrayList` | `LinkedHashSet` |
| Sorted order | use `Collections.sort()` | `TreeSet` |
| Thread-safe | `CopyOnWriteArrayList` | `ConcurrentSkipListSet` |

A practical pattern: use a Set internally but return a List to the caller.
A common pattern is a method like `getUniqueCountries` that takes a list of orders, fills a `LinkedHashSet` with each order's country so duplicates drop but order is preserved, then returns a new `ArrayList` built from that set.

## Internal Implementation Differences

The performance characteristics of Set and List come directly from their underlying data structures. Understanding the internals makes choosing between them automatic.

### HashSet Is a HashMap In Disguise

`HashSet` is literally implemented as a `HashMap<E, Object>` where every value is the same dummy constant (`PRESENT`). When you call `set.add("hello")`, it calls `map.put("hello", PRESENT)`. When you call `set.contains("hello")`, it calls `map.containsKey("hello")`.

```java
// Actual JDK source (simplified)
public class HashSet<E> {
    private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();

    public boolean add(E e) {
        return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null;  // returns false if already exists
    }

    public boolean contains(Object o) {
        return map.containsKey(o);  // O(1) hash lookup
    }
}
```

This means HashSet inherits all of HashMap's characteristics: O(1) average `add`/`contains`/`remove`, initial capacity 16, load factor 0.75, same resizing behavior.

### Why contains() Performance Matters

The biggest practical difference between Set and List is `contains()`:

```java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();  // 100,000 elements
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>();       // 100,000 elements

list.contains("target");  // O(n) — scans every element sequentially
set.contains("target");   // O(1) — single hash lookup
```

For 100,000 elements, that's the difference between checking ~50,000 elements on average vs. 1. If you're checking membership repeatedly (like deduplication or filtering), using a List is orders of magnitude slower.

### LinkedHashSet: Uniqueness + Order

HashSet does not guarantee iteration order — it depends on hash codes and internal structure. `LinkedHashSet` adds a doubly-linked list threading through all entries, maintaining insertion order at the cost of slightly more memory per entry:

```java
Set<String> hash = new HashSet<>();
hash.add("banana"); hash.add("apple"); hash.add("cherry");
System.out.println(hash);  // [banana, cherry, apple] — unpredictable order

Set<String> linked = new LinkedHashSet<>();
linked.add("banana"); linked.add("apple"); linked.add("cherry");
System.out.println(linked);  // [banana, apple, cherry] — insertion order
```

Use LinkedHashSet when you need both uniqueness and predictable iteration.

### TreeSet: Sorted and Navigable

`TreeSet` is backed by a `TreeMap` (red-black tree). It keeps elements in **sorted order** and provides navigation methods like `first()`, `last()`, `headSet()`, `tailSet()`:

```java
TreeSet<Integer> scores = new TreeSet<>();
scores.addAll(List.of(85, 92, 78, 95, 88));
System.out.println(scores);          // [78, 85, 88, 92, 95] — sorted

scores.headSet(90);                   // [78, 85, 88] — elements < 90
scores.tailSet(90);                   // [92, 95] — elements >= 90
scores.subSet(80, 93);                // [85, 88, 92] — range query
```

The trade-off: all operations are O(log n) instead of O(1). Only use TreeSet when you need sorted iteration or range queries.

### Common Deduplication Patterns

The most frequent real-world use of Set is deduplication — removing duplicates from a List while optionally preserving order:

```java
// Remove duplicates, preserve insertion order
List<String> withDupes = List.of("a", "b", "a", "c", "b", "d");
List<String> unique = new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(withDupes));
// Result: [a, b, c, d]

// Remove duplicates from a stream of objects by a property
List<Order> uniqueByCustomer = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Order::getCustomerId,  // key = customer ID (uniqueness criterion)
        o -> o,                // value = the order itself
        (existing, duplicate) -> existing  // keep first occurrence
    ))
    .values().stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

### Choosing the Right Set Implementation

| Implementation | Ordering | Performance | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HashSet` | None | O(1) | Default choice — uniqueness checks, dedup |
| `LinkedHashSet` | Insertion order | O(1) | When you need predictable iteration order |
| `TreeSet` | Sorted (natural or Comparator) | O(log n) | Range queries, sorted output |
| `EnumSet` | Enum declaration order | O(1) bit ops | Sets of enum constants — fastest possible |
| `CopyOnWriteArraySet` | Insertion order | O(n) add | Tiny sets with many reads, few writes |

- HashSet.contains() is O(1) average, ArrayList.contains() is O(n) — for large datasets this is a massive difference
- Set uses equals() and hashCode() to determine uniqueness — your custom objects must override both
- TreeSet keeps elements sorted but operations are O(log n) instead of O(1) — only use when you need sorted iteration
- To convert List → Set (remove duplicates): new HashSet<>(myList)
- List.of() and Set.of() (Java 9+) create immutable collections — useful for constants
